title: PySpark Storage Layout — Senior Recognition Track
description: A 10-exercise senior recognition track for PySpark Storage Layout at GridUnion Continental. Five modules: SLS1 Multi-Team Partition Contracts · SLS2 OPTIMIZE Scheduling and Z-Order Budgets · SLS3 Parquet vs Delta Architectural Choices · SLS4 VACUUM, Time Travel, Reader Coordination · SLS5 Reviewing Layout Decisions.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Senior scenarios describe GridUnion Continental at platform scale (8M+ meters, 6 teams, 4 countries, 30 regions); the CSV is a small sample for schema reference.

tasks.title: The Partition Scheme That Hurts Three Teams

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team owns the silver.positions table — a 2.4TB Delta table partitioned by counterparty_id. Risk's queries filter by counterparty_id and run in 8 seconds. Two other teams query the same table: Reporting filters by trade_date for daily aggregations (45 minutes per query), Compaction filters by region_code for periodic shrink operations (30 minutes per region). Both Reporting and Compaction effectively full-scan because the partition column does not match their filter pattern. Risk's optimization broke the other two teams without anyone noticing — until Compaction's quarterly run timed out the cluster.
description.task: What is the architectural fix that serves all three teams?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Table: silver.positions (Delta, 2.4 TB)

Current Partition: counterparty_id (~80,000 distinct counterparties)

Queries Per Team: {'Risk': 'filter by counterparty_id — 8s/query (good)', 'Reporting': 'filter by trade_date — 45 min/query (full scan)', 'Compaction': 'filter by region_code — 30 min/region (full scan)'}

Table Owner: Risk team (sole writer, but three readers)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Multi-team Delta table where one team's partition choice imposes catastrophic read cost on two other teams

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# silver.positions layout (current)
  partitionBy: (counterparty_id)
  Z-Order:    none
  ~80,000 partition directories
  Average partition size: 30 MB (alarming small-file flavor too)

# Query plans across teams:

# Risk (filter counterparty_id == 'C0042'):
#   PartitionFilters: [(counterparty_id = C0042)]
#   PartitionCount: 1
#   bytesRead: 30 MB

# Reporting (filter trade_date BETWEEN '2025-04-01' AND '2025-04-30'):
#   PartitionFilters: []
#   PushedFilters: [trade_date BETWEEN ...]
#   PartitionCount: 80,000
#   bytesRead: 2.4 TB ← full scan

# Compaction (filter region_code == 'EU-CENTRAL'):
#   PartitionFilters: []
#   PartitionCount: 80,000
#   bytesRead: 2.4 TB ← full scan

fields.label: What is the architectural fix that serves all three teams?
options: Move silver.positions to be Reporting-team-owned and partition by trade_date instead. Risk and Compaction adapt to the new layout. Owner change resolves the disagreement; majority-team query pattern wins.

Repartition by (trade_date, region_code) — both other teams' filter columns. Add Z-ORDER BY (counterparty_id) for Risk's pattern. Pruning works for date and region; Z-order skipping works for counterparty. All three teams benefit.

Keep counterparty_id partitioning but materialize two extra views: silver_positions_by_date (partitioned by trade_date) and silver_positions_by_region (partitioned by region_code). Each team queries the view that matches their filter.

Add bucketBy(200, 'trade_date') and bucketBy(200, 'region_code') on top of the existing counterparty_id partitioning. Bucketing by all three columns simultaneously gives every team shuffle-skip on their joins.
fields.correctAnswer: Repartition by (trade_date, region_code) — both other teams' filter columns. Add Z-ORDER BY (counterparty_id) for Risk's pattern. Pruning works for date and region; Z-order skipping works for counterparty. All three teams benefit.
fields.rationale: The right architectural fix combines partitioning (for the columns that benefit most from directory-level pruning) with Z-ordering (for the column.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats team ownership as the lever.The data is shared; ownership change does not fix shared layout.4TB scale.

tasks.pssReference: PSS3 lesson 4 (Multi-Team Lakehouse Architecture), PSS3 lesson 5 (Layout Choices Across Teams).

tasks.title: Per-Team Partition Divergence — When Allowed

description.context: After SLS1.1, GridUnion's architecture council debates how to GOVERN partition schemes across the lakehouse. Two architectural patterns are on the table. Pattern A: Platform mandates a SINGLE uniform partition scheme for shared tables (e.g., all silver tables MUST partitionBy(date, region)) — uniformity wins. Pattern B: Per-team divergence ALLOWED with documented contracts in catalog metadata — flexibility wins. Both have merit. The architect must identify which fits which lakehouse maturity stage.
description.task: Which pattern fits which lakehouse maturity stage?

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two architectural governance models compared for partition-scheme management across teams

evidence.label: Pattern A — Enforced uniform partitioning
evidence.content:
# Platform invariant (enforced via CI):
# All silver tables MUST partitionBy(date, region)
#   Default partition scheme for new tables
#   Existing tables migrated within 90 days
#   Deviation requires architecture-council exception

# Pros:
#   - Predictable cross-team query performance
#   - One pattern to document, one to teach
#   - Cross-team joins benefit from aligned partitions
# Cons:
#   - Forces some teams onto suboptimal layouts for their dominant queries
#   - Cannot exploit team-specific access patterns

evidence.label: Pattern B — Per-team divergence with contracts
evidence.content:
# Platform allows divergence; requires contract in catalog:
#   ALTER TABLE silver.foo SET TBLPROPERTIES (
#     'partition.scheme.rationale' = 'team-x-primary-filter',
#     'partition.scheme.consumers'  = 'team-x',
#     'partition.scheme.affects'    = 'team-y, team-z',
#     'partition.scheme.review.next' = '2026-Q3'
#   )

# Pros:
#   - Each table optimized for its primary use case
#   - Trade-offs explicit in metadata, reviewable
# Cons:
#   - Cross-team joins more variable in performance
#   - Requires governance discipline (review cadence)
#   - Complex for new engineers to learn

fields.label: Which pattern fits which lakehouse maturity stage?
options: Pattern A always wins. Uniformity is the only sustainable path; per-team divergence inevitably degrades into inconsistency. Mature lakehouses converge to uniform partitioning regardless of team count.
Pattern B always wins. Modern lakehouses are flexible by design; uniformity sacrifices too much per-team performance gain. Pattern A is a 2010s anti-pattern that mature lakehouses outgrew.

Pattern A fits early-stage lakehouses (few teams) where consistency dominates and bad layouts cost a lot. Pattern B fits mature lakehouses where contracts are reviewable and divergence costs are managed.
Both patterns are equivalent in practice; the labels are different but the runtime behavior is identical. Choose based on team naming preference or whichever feels familiar to the team.
fields.correctAnswer: Pattern A fits early-stage lakehouses (few teams) where consistency dominates and bad layouts cost a lot. Pattern B fits mature lakehouses where contracts are reviewable and divergence costs are managed.
fields.rationale: The choice is stage-dependent.1 case).Uniformity prevents the disaster.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats uniformity as universally correct; ignores per-team optimization value at scale.

tasks.pssReference: PSS3 lesson 5 (Layout Governance Models), PSS9 lesson 6 (Cross-Team Architecture Maturity).

tasks.title: Three Teams, One OPTIMIZE Window

description.context: GridUnion's silver.positions Delta table receives OPTIMIZE bi-weekly during the maintenance window — one full pass per fortnight is all the cluster can sustain. Three teams want different Z-order column choices. Risk wants ZORDER BY (counterparty_id, trade_date) for portfolio queries. Reporting wants ZORDER BY (region_code, date) for daily summaries. Compaction wants no Z-order at all (their full-scan operations don't benefit, and Z-order rewrite slows their data ingest). The OPTIMIZE budget is one column-choice per fortnight. The architect must allocate.
description.task: Which Z-order allocation is the right architectural call, and why?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Table: silver.positions (2.4 TB, Delta)

Optimize Budget: 1 full-table OPTIMIZE per fortnight (4 hours of cluster time)

Current Partition: (date, region) — agreed across teams

Team Requests: {'Risk': 'ZORDER BY (counterparty_id, trade_date) — 200 portfolio queries/day, current p99 = 12s', 'Reporting': 'ZORDER BY (region_code, date) — 8 daily summaries, current p99 = 45min', 'Compaction': 'NO ZORDER — slower writes, no read benefit'}

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Three competing Z-ORDER BY requests for a shared Delta table with limited OPTIMIZE compute budget

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Quantitative impact analysis (projected by architect)

# Option Risk-favored: ZORDER BY (counterparty_id, trade_date)
#   Risk:       12s -> 4s   (3x improvement)  × 200 queries/day = 1600s/day saved
#   Reporting:  45min -> 45min (no change)
#   Compaction: writes -8% slower (Z-order rewrite cost)
#   Daily team-time saved: 1600s = ~27 min for Risk

# Option Reporting-favored: ZORDER BY (region_code, date)
#   Risk:       12s -> 12s   (no change)
#   Reporting:  45min -> 9min (5x improvement)  × 8 queries/day = 17,280s/day saved
#   Compaction: writes -8% slower
#   Daily team-time saved: 17,280s = ~288 min for Reporting

# Option Compaction-favored: no ZORDER
#   Risk:       12s -> 12s
#   Reporting:  45min -> 45min
#   Compaction: writes baseline
#   Daily team-time saved: 0

fields.label: Which Z-order allocation is the right architectural call, and why?
options: Risk wins. 200 portfolio queries/day is the highest query volume; the team using the table most often dictates the layout. Z-order on (counterparty_id, trade_date) maximizes total queries served. Reporting and Compaction adapt to slower runtimes.

Reporting wins. Daily team-time saved (288 minutes) is 10× larger than Risk's (27 minutes). Total cluster value is maximized by the largest aggregate gain. ZORDER BY (region_code, date). Document the trade-off in the catalog so Risk knows their layer is suboptimal.

Alternate fortnightly: week 1 Z-order favors Risk, week 2 favors Reporting. Rolling alternation gives both teams half-time benefit. Compaction's write slowdown is constant across both schemes regardless of choice.

Compaction wins. Their write-side slowdown affects every team's data freshness; readers depend on fresh writes. Avoiding the 8% write penalty preserves cluster throughput. Both readers accept slower queries; data freshness is the platform invariant.
fields.correctAnswer: Reporting wins. Daily team-time saved (288 minutes) is 10× larger than Risk's (27 minutes). Total cluster value is maximized by the largest aggregate gain. ZORDER BY (region_code, date). Document the trade-off in the catalog so Risk knows their layer is suboptimal.
fields.rationale: The senior architectural call optimizes for total team-time saved, not query count.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Conflates query count with team-time impact; total time saved is the optimization target.

tasks.pssReference: PSS3 lesson 6 (OPTIMIZE Budget Allocation Across Teams).

tasks.title: Z-Order on a Mutable Table — Drift Pattern

description.context: GridUnion's silver.positions has been Z-ordered for 3 weeks. The OPTIMIZE was effective when run — file-skipping dropped query times from 45 minutes to 9 minutes. But the table is appended-to daily by the data ingest pipeline. After 3 weeks of appends, Reporting's queries hit a BIMODAL latency distribution: queries on data older than the last OPTIMIZE run in 9 minutes (Z-order working); queries on the recent 21 days run in 45 minutes (Z-order doesn't help on unsorted appended files). The Z-ORDER itself is fine; what's broken is the contract between OPTIMIZE frequency and data freshness expectations.
description.task: What is the architectural diagnosis and the right fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Table: silver.positions (Delta)

Z Order Columns: (region_code, date)

Optimize Cadence: every 14 days (fortnightly)

Append Cadence: daily (data ingest pipeline)

Last Optimize: 21 days ago

Observation: queries on data >21 days old run in 9 min (Z-order working); queries on data ≤21 days old run in 45 min (Z-order missing)

Files In Table: 1,200 total (800 Z-ordered, 400 unsorted appends)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Bimodal-latency Delta table where Z-order helped historically but daily appends drift the layout — fortnightly OPTIMIZE cadence is too slow

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Per-file metadata (representative sample)

File part-00037-z-ordered.parquet:
  written: 2025-04-13 (during last OPTIMIZE)
  z-order:    yes — clustered by (region_code, date)
  min/max:    region: NORTH-only,  date: 2025-04-01..2025-04-12

File part-00800-append-2025-04-30.parquet:
  written: 2025-04-30 (daily append)
  z-order:    no — append rows scattered across regions/dates
  min/max:    region: NORTH..WEST,  date: 2025-04-30 only

# Query: filter(date BETWEEN '2025-05-01' AND '2025-05-04') — recent week
#   numFilesTotal:                  1,200
#   numFilesRead (Z-ordered files):     2  (high min/max selectivity)
#   numFilesRead (append files):      400  (no min/max selectivity)
#   Total: 402 files read for what should be a 4-day query

fields.label: What is the architectural diagnosis and the right fix?
options: OPTIMIZE cadence does not match append cadence. Fix is incremental OPTIMIZE on recent partitions only. Run daily on date > current_date - 14 ZORDER BY region_code and date. Full-table OPTIMIZE moves to quarterly.

Z-order is the wrong optimization for mutable tables; only static reference tables benefit. Convert silver.positions to use bucketBy(200, region_code) instead — bucket layout survives appends without rewrite.

The append pipeline is the bug — it should run INSERT OVERWRITE instead of INSERT INTO so each new day rewrites and re-Z-orders the affected files. Fix: change the ingest job's write semantics permanently.

The 45-minute query time on recent data is correct and expected; recent data is always slower in Delta because of transaction-log overhead on new writes. The bimodal pattern resolves itself once data ages past the log compaction window.
fields.correctAnswer: OPTIMIZE cadence does not match append cadence. Fix is incremental OPTIMIZE on recent partitions only. Run daily on date > current_date - 14 ZORDER BY region_code and date. Full-table OPTIMIZE moves to quarterly.
fields.rationale: The OPTIMIZE cadence vs append cadence mismatch is the architectural failure.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Conflates Z-order with static-only optimization; rolling OPTIMIZE makes Z-order viable for mutable tables.

tasks.pssReference: PSS3 lesson 7 (Rolling OPTIMIZE for Mutable Delta Tables).

tasks.title: Parquet Bronze, Delta Silver — The Schema Divergence

description.context: GridUnion's lakehouse uses a layered architecture. bronze.events_raw is plain Parquet (immutable, append-only, ingest landing zone). silver.events_clean is Delta (mutable, schema-evolved, downstream consumption layer). 6 weeks ago, Risk team added a new column 'risk_classification' to silver.events_clean via ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN. The Parquet bronze upstream was NOT updated. The silver-to-gold pipeline reads from bronze through silver, and the new column is null for all rows whose bronze source predates the silver schema change. Risk's reports show 6 weeks of nulls. The architect reads the Delta transaction log entries to identify the gap.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Bronze Format: parquet (append-only, no schema control)

Silver Format: delta (schema-evolved 6 weeks ago)

Schema Change: ALTER TABLE silver.events_clean ADD COLUMN risk_classification STRING

Current State: silver has the new column, bronze does not

Downstream Observation: risk_classification is null for all rows from bronze data older than 6 weeks

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Parquet bronze + Delta silver layered architecture where schema evolution on silver was not propagated upstream — schema divergence visible in Delta transaction log

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Delta transaction log entry (silver.events_clean, 6 weeks ago)
_delta_log/00000000000000128.json:
  {
    "commitInfo": {
      "operation": "ADD COLUMNS",
      "operationParameters": {
        "columns": [{"name": "risk_classification", "type": "string"}]
      }
    }
  }

# Bronze parquet schema (current, unchanged):
  describe bronze.events_raw
  +------------------+--------+
  | event_id         | string |
  | counterparty_id  | string |
  | trade_date       | date   |
  | exposure         | double |
  +------------------+--------+
  (no risk_classification column)

# Silver-to-gold pipeline:
#   reads bronze.events_raw (4 columns)
#   reads silver.events_clean (5 columns including risk_classification)
#   joins them on event_id
#   risk_classification is null for any event_id present in bronze but not in silver

fields.label: What is the architectural diagnosis?
options: The schema evolution was applied to the wrong layer — silver should not be Delta; the schema change should have been applied to bronze. Fix: revert silver.events_clean to plain parquet and add the column to bronze instead.

Schema evolution on silver is correct, but the upstream bronze schema must update synchronously. Adding columns to silver alone produces null backfill across all historical bronze rows whenever the join runs.

Delta tables with schema evolution must be paired with an explicit schema-version policy; the silver table should store a schema_version column and downstream queries filter on it. Fix: add schema_version to silver.events_clean and partition by it.

Schema evolution on silver is correct, but the upstream bronze schema must update synchronously. Adding columns to silver alone produces null backfill. Fix: amend bronze.events_raw schema OR write a backfill job for risk_classification.
fields.correctAnswer: Schema evolution on silver is correct, but the upstream bronze schema must update synchronously. Adding columns to silver alone produces null backfill. Fix: amend bronze.events_raw schema OR write a backfill job for risk_classification.
fields.rationale: The architectural failure is that schema evolution was applied to one layer without coordinating the upstream source.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Reverts the layered architecture; silver-as-Delta is correct, the change semantics are the issue.

tasks.pssReference: PSS4 lesson 5 (Delta Schema Evolution Across Layers), PSS3 lesson 8 (Lakehouse Layered Architecture Coordination).

tasks.title: Time-Travel Cost on a Hot Table

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team uses Delta time-travel to pin SLA-critical reports to the prior month's snapshot — a common compliance pattern. The query syntax is spark.read.format('delta').option('timestampAsOf', '2025-04-01').load('silver.positions'). Time-travel works by reading the transaction log to reconstruct the file list as it existed at that timestamp. silver.positions has been written-to daily for 4 years; the _delta_log directory contains 4 million+ entries. Resolving the time-travel reference now takes 12+ minutes per query, before any actual data is read. Risk's morning reports are missing SLAs.
description.task: What is the architectural fix for time-travel SLA degradation?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Table: silver.positions

Table Age: 4 years

Delta Log Entries: ~4 million

Log Size On Disk: 180 GB

Time Travel Resolution Time: 12-14 minutes per query

Actual Data Read Time: 8-15 minutes after resolution

Sla Target: 10 minutes total

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Delta table with massive transaction-log history; time-travel queries spend most of their time resolving log entries, not reading data

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# _delta_log/ structure (silver.positions)
  00000000000000000000.json     ← initial commit, 4 years ago
  00000000000000000001.json
  ...
  00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet  ← every 10 commits, default
  00000000000000000011.json
  ...
  00000000000003999999.json
  00000000000004000000.checkpoint.parquet

  _last_checkpoint                     ← points to 4000000.checkpoint
  Total: ~4M JSON files + ~400K checkpoints + 180 GB log size

# Time-travel query: spark.read.option('timestampAsOf', '2025-04-01').load(...)
#   Step 1: Find checkpoint at-or-before 2025-04-01      (fast, _last_checkpoint helps)
#   Step 2: Replay JSON commits from checkpoint to target (SLOW — many small reads)
#   Step 3: Reconstruct file list                          (memory pressure)
#   Step 4: Actual data read                               (8-15 min)
#
# Steps 1-3: 12-14 minutes — DOMINATES the query time

fields.label: What is the architectural fix for time-travel SLA degradation?
options: Increase Delta checkpoint frequency from every 10 commits to every 1 commit; shorter chains between checkpoints means faster resolution. Fix: spark.databricks.delta.checkpointInterval=1 in cluster config.
Increase Delta checkpoint frequency from every 10 commits to every 1 commit; shorter chains between checkpoints means faster resolution. Fix: spark.databricks.delta.checkpointInterval=1.

Drop time-travel for SLA paths. Replace with explicit snapshot tables — every month, materialize silver.positions_2025_04 as a frozen copy. Risk's reports query the copy. Eliminates log-resolution overhead.

Schedule periodic log compaction via VACUUM with deepClone; this consolidates the transaction log into fewer entries while preserving the time-travel capability. Fix: nightly VACUUM with retention=400 days.
fields.correctAnswer: Drop time-travel for SLA paths. Replace with explicit snapshot tables — every month, materialize silver.positions_2025_04 as a frozen copy. Risk's reports query the copy. Eliminates log-resolution overhead.
fields.rationale: Time-travel resolution scales with log size.At 4M entries, even with checkpoints, replay dominates.The architectural fix depends on the use case.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats log replay as parallelizable; it is sequential by commit ordering.

tasks.pssReference: PSS4 lesson 6 (Delta Transaction Log Internals), PSS3 lesson 9 (Snapshot Tables for SLA-Critical Time-Travel).

tasks.title: VACUUM Stranded a Reader

description.context: GridUnion's Operations team ran VACUUM on silver.positions with the default 7-day retention to reclaim storage. Risk team had a long-running portfolio analysis that started 8 days earlier — the query was still resolving when VACUUM physically deleted the parquet files it was about to read. Risk's query failed with FileNotFoundException. The two teams have no coordination protocol for VACUUM cadence vs reader lifecycle. The architect must identify the cross-team contract gap and design the fix.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Incident: Risk's portfolio analysis failed with FileNotFoundException after 8.5 hours of execution

Vacuum Command: VACUUM silver.positions RETAIN 168 HOURS

Vacuum Retention Default: 7 days (168 hours)

Risk Query Start: 2025-05-04 02:00 UTC

Vacuum Run Start: 2025-05-04 04:00 UTC (Operations cron)

Files Deleted: 1,840 files older than 7 days

Risk Query Was Reading: files written 2025-04-26 (8 days old)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Cross-team incident where VACUUM physically deleted files mid-read, breaking a long-running query — coordination gap visible in incident timeline

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Incident timeline
02:00  Risk submits portfolio analysis (silver.positions read pinned to snapshot at submit time)
02:15  Query reads first 200 files (the day's hot data)
04:00  Operations cron triggers nightly VACUUM (default 7-day retention)
04:08  VACUUM physically deletes 1,840 parquet files older than 2025-04-26 (7 days)
10:34  Risk's query reaches files written 2025-04-26 — files no longer exist on disk
10:34  java.io.FileNotFoundException: silver.positions/part-00417-...parquet

# What Delta normally protects:
#   - Commit-time isolation: query sees consistent snapshot ✓
#   - File availability: depends on VACUUM retention vs query duration ✗

# VACUUM does not check for active readers; it physically deletes files
# whose tombstones are older than the retention threshold.

fields.label: What is the architectural fix?
options: Operations should not run VACUUM during business hours. Fix: schedule VACUUM only during the maintenance window (Sunday 02:00-04:00) and announce 24h in advance via team-channel notification. No reader-coordination protocol needed.

VACUUM is incompatible with long-running readers; switch to time-travel-only retention (delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration='interval 30 days'). Risk's queries pin via timestampAsOf instead of relying on file availability.

Risk's query is the bug — 8.5-hour analysis queries should not exist on a hot table. Fix: split the analysis into smaller chunks that complete within 1 hour each, eliminating the cross-VACUUM-window risk entirely.

Increase VACUUM retention to 30 days as a platform invariant. Long-running queries (>7 days) become tolerable. Storage cost grows but stranded-reader incidents stop. Reader-pinning is enforced via VACUUM retention, not coordination.
fields.correctAnswer: Increase VACUUM retention to 30 days as a platform invariant. Long-running queries (>7 days) become tolerable. Storage cost grows but stranded-reader incidents stop. Reader-pinning is enforced via VACUUM retention, not coordination.
fields.rationale: The architectural fix raises VACUUM retention to bound the maximum query duration.30 days is the standard for shared analytical lakehouses.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Coordination protocols are fragile; platform invariants are more robust.

tasks.pssReference: PSS4 lesson 7 (Delta VACUUM and Reader Coordination), PSS9 lesson 6 (Cross-Team Maintenance Contracts).

tasks.title: Time-Travel Versus VACUUM Retention

description.context: GridUnion's Operations team proposes two VACUUM retention configurations for silver.positions. Configuration A: aggressive 1-day retention. Saves storage cost (only 1 day of tombstoned files retained) but kills time-travel beyond 1 day and creates the SLS4.1 stranded-reader scenario. Configuration B: conservative 30-day retention. Preserves time-travel up to 30 days, supports long-running readers, but balloons storage cost (30 days of tombstones × daily-write churn = ~30× more storage for the same logical data). The architect must pick given specific team requirements.
description.task: Which configuration is the right architectural choice?

evidence.title: Input sample
Dataset
evidence.content: Two VACUUM retention configurations compared for storage cost vs time-travel and reader-coordination implications

evidence.label: Configuration A — Aggressive 1-day retention
evidence.content:
VACUUM silver.positions RETAIN 24 HOURS
# Storage retained for tombstoned files: ~120 GB (1 day × daily churn)
# Time-travel: 1 day max (older snapshots cannot be reconstructed)
# Reader window: 24 hours max (queries longer than 1 day fail)

# Pros:
#   - Minimal storage overhead
# Cons:
#   - Risk loses 30-day compliance time-travel ✗
#   - Reporting's 4-6 hour queries safe but no margin
#   - Compliance's 7-day rollback impossible ✗

evidence.label: Configuration B — Conservative 30-day retention
evidence.content:
VACUUM silver.positions RETAIN 720 HOURS
# Storage retained for tombstoned files: ~3.6 TB (30 days × daily churn)
# Time-travel: 30 days
# Reader window: 30 days

# Pros:
#   - Risk's compliance reporting works ✓
#   - Reporting's queries safe ✓
#   - Compliance's 7-day rollback works ✓
# Cons:
#   - 3.6 TB of tombstoned-file storage
#   - Operations storage quota strained further (currently at 80%)

fields.label: Which configuration is the right architectural choice?
options: Configuration A wins. Storage cost is the platform's primary constraint at 80% quota; aggressive VACUUM is the only sustainable option. Risk and Compliance must adapt their requirements to the platform's storage budget. Storage drives architecture.

Neither — split silver.positions into two tables: silver.positions_hot (1-day retention for Operations frugality) and silver.positions_cold (30-day retention for Risk/Compliance). Each team queries the appropriate table. Storage and compliance both addressed.

Neither — split silver.positions into silver.positions_hot (1-day for Operations frugality) and silver.positions_cold (30-day for Risk/Compliance). Each team queries the appropriate table. Storage and compliance both addressed.

Configuration B wins. Storage is cheap relative to compliance and SLA failures. The 3.6 TB cost is bounded; Risk's compliance miss and Compliance's regulatory failure are unbounded business risk. Storage quota expansion is the right response, not retention reduction.
fields.correctAnswer: Configuration B wins. Storage is cheap relative to compliance and SLA failures. The 3.6 TB cost is bounded; Risk's compliance miss and Compliance's regulatory failure are unbounded business risk. Storage quota expansion is the right response, not retention reduction.
fields.rationale: The senior call evaluates relative cost.6TB at modern cloud rates (~$80/month) is bounded and small.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats storage as architectural primary; cost asymmetry says otherwise.

tasks.pssReference: PSS4 lesson 7 (VACUUM Retention Policies), PSS9 lesson 6 (Cost-Asymmetry Architectural Reasoning).

tasks.title: Reviewing a Layout Proposal

description.context: GridUnion's Reporting team senior submitted a pull request to rebalance silver.aggregations — change partition scheme from (date) to (date, region_code), add ZORDER BY (customer_type, daily_kw), reduce VACUUM retention from 30 days to 7 days. Risk team's architect reviews. The PR's stated goal is to speed up Reporting's 8 daily summary queries. The architect must check four cross-team risk dimensions: upstream contract impact, downstream optimization unlock, migration cost, and rollback path.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Cross-team layout-rebalance PR with four review dimensions to evaluate

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# PR: rebalance-silver-aggregations
# Author: Reporting team senior

# Changes proposed:
#   1. ALTER TABLE silver.aggregations PARTITIONED BY (date, region_code)
#      Was:  partitionBy(date)        — 365 partitions
#      To:   partitionBy(date, region_code)  — 365 × 4 = 1460 partitions
#
#   2. OPTIMIZE silver.aggregations ZORDER BY (customer_type, daily_kw)
#      Net effect: file-skipping on Reporting's customer_type filter pattern
#
#   3. ALTER TABLE silver.aggregations SET TBLPROPERTIES (
#        'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 7 days'
#      )
#      Was:  30 days  →  To:  7 days

# Cross-team usage:
#   Reporting: 8 daily summary queries — primary beneficiary
#   Risk:      pinned time-travel reads — depends on 30-day retention
#   Compaction: nightly maintenance — reads partition layout for incremental work
#   Audit:     30-day rollback for compliance — depends on 30-day retention

# Migration plan in PR:
#   - Run ALTER TABLE on silver.aggregations in maintenance window
#   - Re-OPTIMIZE entire table (estimated 8 hours, 4 TB rewrite)
#   - VACUUM with new 7-day retention immediately after

fields.label: Q1 — Does Change #1 (partition scheme change) break upstream or downstream contracts?
options: Yes — Compaction's nightly job reads partition layout for incremental processing. Changing from (date) to (date, region_code) means Compaction sees 4× more partitions per night. Coordination required before merge.
No — partition scheme changes are local to the table; they don't affect upstream or downstream consumers in any way. The PR is safe to merge without coordination overhead.
No, but only because (date, region_code) preserves date as the leading partition column. If region_code came first, downstream would break. The current ordering is safe.

Yes — Reporting's queries that filter on date alone will read 4× more partitions because the leading partition column is unchanged. The change actively HARMS Reporting's queries while supposedly helping them.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — Compaction's nightly job reads partition layout for incremental processing. Changing from (date) to (date, region_code) means Compaction sees 4× more partitions per night. Coordination required before merge.
fields.rationale: Compaction's incremental logic reads partition_id from the file system to track 'what's new since last run'.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats partition changes as local; they affect every consumer of partition_id.

fields.label: Q2 — Does Change #2 (ZORDER BY customer_type, daily_kw) interact with Change #1's partition scheme?
options: Yes, harmfully. Z-order conflicts with multi-column partitioning. The OPTIMIZE rewrite breaks the partition spec; queries fail until manual repartitioning is applied.
Yes, harmfully. Z-order conflicts with multi-column partitioning. The OPTIMIZE rewrite breaks the partition spec; queries fail until manual repartitioning.
Yes, beneficially. With (date, region_code) partitioning, each partition is small. Z-order on customer_type creates fine-grained file-skipping within each partition.
Yes, but only if customer_type is added as a third partition column. Otherwise Z-order on customer_type is a no-op because partition pruning hides it from the file-skipping evaluator.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes, beneficially. With (date, region_code) partitioning, each partition is small. Z-order on customer_type creates fine-grained file-skipping within each partition.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats them as independent; Z-order's effectiveness depends on partition size.

fields.label: Q3 — Change #3 (VACUUM retention 30→7 days): what is the risk?
options: No risk — 7 days is reasonable VACUUM retention; storage savings outweigh marginal coordination cost. Most lakehouses run with 7-day retention as the default policy.

Risk's pinned time-travel breaks — needs 30-day retention. Audit's 30-day rollback breaks — regulatory requirement. Reject or split the change: keep retention at 30 days, address Reporting separately.
Risk is moderate — Audit's 30-day rollback fails on day 8 onward, but only triggers if regulators audit during that window (statistically rare). Accept the risk for the storage savings.

Risk is bidirectional — Reporting's own 4-6 hour queries become exposed to stranded-reader incidents if any individual query exceeds 7 days. The PR fix protects against the team that submitted it as well.
fields.correctAnswer: Risk's pinned time-travel breaks — needs 30-day retention. Audit's 30-day rollback breaks — regulatory requirement. Reject or split the change: keep retention at 30 days, address Reporting separately.
fields.rationale: 30→7 day retention reduction is the most dangerous change in this PR.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats the retention change as local; it directly violates Audit's regulatory requirement.

fields.label: Q4 — What is the rollback path if the PR is merged and proves problematic?
options: Rollback is easy — ALTER TABLE undoes the partition change in seconds; VACUUM retention is reversed by another ALTER TABLE. Only Z-order is irreversible (the rewrite is one-way), but a future OPTIMIZE without ZORDER BY restores the prior layout.

Rollback is impossible — once the partition scheme is changed, the data is physically reorganized. The only path is to recreate the table from bronze sources (8+ hours, all consumers offline). Rollback risk is the dominant review consideration.

Rollback is partial. Partition reverts via ALTER + full rewrite (~8h). Z-order reverts via OPTIMIZE without ZORDER (~8h). VACUUM retention reverts but already-deleted files are gone forever. Total: ~16h plus permanent loss.

Rollback path is the same as forward path — run the inverse PR with reversed parameters. Cost is symmetric, ~8 hours either direction. No special consideration needed for the review process beyond standard rebalance.
fields.correctAnswer: Rollback is partial. Partition reverts via ALTER + full rewrite (~8h). Z-order reverts via OPTIMIZE without ZORDER (~8h). VACUUM retention reverts but already-deleted files are gone forever. Total: ~16h plus permanent loss.
fields.rationale: Each change has a different rollback profile.Partition scheme: revert via ALTER TABLE + full table rewrite (8 hours of cluster time).
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Underestimates rewrite cost (8 hours per change) and treats VACUUM deletions as reversible.

tasks.title: Quarterly Lakehouse Rebalance Audit

description.context: Final SLS exercise. GridUnion's quarterly lakehouse rebalance plan has 4 proposed changes spanning 4 different shared tables. The architect audits the plan for cross-team safety, ordering dependencies, rollback risk, and which changes need upstream contract amendments. Each sub-question addresses a different aspect of multi-team rebalance coordination.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Quarterly multi-pipeline lakehouse rebalance plan with 4 layout changes affecting 6 teams

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# 2026 Q2 LAKEHOUSE REBALANCE PLAN

# Change 1 — silver.positions: partition scheme MURMUR3 → XXHASH64
#   Driver: Spark 3.5 default (XXHASH64 is faster)
#   Effect: every partition_id changes; ~2.4 TB rewrite
#   Affected: Risk (writer), Compaction (incremental reader), Reporting (some incremental jobs)

# Change 2 — silver.events_clean: Z-ORDER recolumn
#   From: ZORDER BY (counterparty_id, trade_date)
#   To:   ZORDER BY (region_code, trade_date)
#   Driver: Reporting team's query mix shifted; counterparty filters dropped to 5%
#   Effect: 1.8 TB rewrite
#   Affected: Reporting (beneficiary), Risk (regression risk)

# Change 3 — silver.regional_dim: VACUUM retention 30 → 90 days
#   Driver: Audit team's compliance requirements expanded
#   Effect: ~6× storage growth for tombstoned files (~80 GB more)
#   Affected: Audit (beneficiary), Operations (storage quota)

# Change 4 — silver.aggregations: bucket count 50 → 200
#   Driver: customer_dim's bucket-aware joins are 4× the original scale
#   Effect: full table rewrite (~3 TB)
#   Affected: 4 teams that join against aggregations; bucket-count must align

# Architectural review checkpoint: cross-team safety + ordering + rollback + contracts

fields.label: Q1 — Change #1 (MURMUR3 → XXHASH64): cross-team impact and required coordination?
options: Change #1 is a downstream-contract violation. Compaction's incremental processing reads partition_id; XXHASH64 produces different ids than MURMUR3. Compaction reprocesses 100% on first post-change run. Coordinate before the window.
Change #1 is benign; Spark handles hash function transitions transparently. Compaction reads from filesystem, not partition_id; the rename is invisible to consumers. Proceed without coordination.

Change #1 must be deferred until Spark 4.0 release; XXHASH64 has known incompatibilities with Spark 3.5's bucketing logic. The rebalance plan's stated driver is incorrect for the current cluster version.

Change #1 fully deprecates the Spark 3.4 cluster path; both writers and readers must upgrade to 3.5 simultaneously. Coordinate the cluster-wide upgrade as a separate ticket; Change #1 itself is a no-op until that completes.
fields.correctAnswer: Change #1 is a downstream-contract violation. Compaction's incremental processing reads partition_id; XXHASH64 produces different ids than MURMUR3. Compaction reprocesses 100% on first post-change run. Coordinate before the window.
fields.rationale: 2 Q1.Compaction's incremental skip logic implicitly contracted on partition_id stability.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats hash rename as transparent; partition_id is the actual contract surface.5 incompatibility not in the scenario.

fields.label: Q2 — Change #2 (Z-ORDER recolumn): is the rationale sound, and what is the rollback risk?
options: Rationale is sound — query mix shifted from counterparty_id to region_code. Rollback risk: 1.8 TB rewrite is one-way; if Risk regresses, rollback is another 1.8 TB rewrite. Track Risk's p99 for 2 weeks.
Rationale is unsound — Z-order on a new column is rarely worth the rewrite. Risk's 5% remaining counterparty queries will degrade severely after the change. Reject Change #2.
Rationale is sound but the recolumn should add region_code WITHOUT removing counterparty_id: ZORDER BY (region_code, trade_date, counterparty_id). Three-column Z-order maintains both query patterns.
Z-order changes are immune to rollback risk because OPTIMIZE preserves the prior layout in the transaction log. Risk can time-travel to the pre-OPTIMIZE state if their queries regress.
fields.correctAnswer: Rationale is sound — query mix shifted from counterparty_id to region_code. Rollback risk: 1.8 TB rewrite is one-way; if Risk regresses, rollback is another 1.8 TB rewrite. Track Risk's p99 for 2 weeks.
fields.rationale: Z-order recolumn rationale is sound when query mix shifts.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats Z-order recolumn as universally bad; it's the right response to query mix shifts.

fields.label: Q3 — Change #3 (VACUUM 30→90 days, ~80GB storage growth): the asymmetry calculus from SLS4.2 applies — what is the call?
options: Defer to Operations team — Operations owns the storage budget and the call is theirs. Audit team works with Operations to find a solution; the architect doesn't have authority to approve the change.

Reject. Storage cost compounds — every regulator-driven retention extension grows storage further. Set a precedent: regulatory requirements must be met by specialized snapshot tables, not by extending shared-table retention.

Approve conditionally — extend retention only on compliance-relevant partitions, not the full table. Use ALTER TABLE silver.regional_dim PARTITION (compliance=true) SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration'='90 days').
Approve. 80GB at modern cloud rates is ~$2/month. Audit's expanded compliance requirements are unbounded business risk. Bounded small cost vs unbounded risk: trivial decision in favor of compliance.
fields.correctAnswer: Approve. 80GB at modern cloud rates is ~$2/month. Audit's expanded compliance requirements are unbounded business risk. Bounded small cost vs unbounded risk: trivial decision in favor of compliance.
fields.rationale: 2 cost-asymmetry framework.80GB storage at cloud rates is trivial; Audit's compliance failure is unbounded.The senior call is approve, not deny.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Defers architectural authority; the architect signs off on cross-team trade-offs.

fields.label: Q4 — Change #4 (bucket count 50→200): cross-team alignment requirement?
options: Alignment is one-directional — only consumers writing to silver.aggregations need to update; consumers reading are unaffected because read-time bucket-skip works on either side independently.
No alignment needed — Spark auto-rehashes bucket counts at query time when joining tables with mismatched bucket counts. The 4 consuming teams are unaffected by the change.
Critical alignment — the 4 teams that join silver.aggregations must ALSO change their bucket counts to 200. Otherwise SLS2.2's bucket-mismatch silent regression hits all 4 teams.
Bucket count change is purely metadata; the underlying parquet files don't move. Spark uses bucket spec metadata for runtime decisions but file layout is stable. The plan's effect estimate is wrong.
fields.correctAnswer: Critical alignment — the 4 teams that join silver.aggregations must ALSO change their bucket counts to 200. Otherwise SLS2.2's bucket-mismatch silent regression hits all 4 teams.
fields.rationale: 2 — both sides of any bucketed join must have matching bucket counts or Spark silently disables bucket-skip.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats read-side as immune; reads with mismatched buckets shuffle silently.

fields.label: Q5 — Looking at all four changes, what is the right ORDERING and which need upstream contract amendments?
options: All four can run in parallel during the same maintenance window; cluster has capacity for the load. Save 50% of total time by parallelizing all changes together.
Sequential start with retention. Then Z-order. Then bucket alignment. Then hash function last. Contracts: hash function needs Compaction amendment; bucket count needs all 4 consumer amendments.
Reverse order — start with the largest rewrite (#1 at 2.4 TB) to fail-fast if cluster issues arise. Smaller changes are quick recovery if anything goes wrong early.
Order doesn't matter; ordering is a project-management concern, not architectural. The architect signs off on each independently and Operations schedules them.
fields.correctAnswer: Sequential start with retention. Then Z-order. Then bucket alignment. Then hash function last. Contracts: hash function needs Compaction amendment; bucket count needs all 4 consumer amendments.
fields.rationale: Sequential ordering is required because each change has different prerequisite contracts.#3 (retention) is fastest and lowest-risk — start there.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Parallel execution misses cross-change dependencies.
